strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem regarding the reliability of widely-used LLM evaluation platforms, with practical implications for the community
Sound methodological approach using theoretically grounded AMIP framework; the reduction to pairwise comparisons (Proposition 3.1) is elegant and mathematically principled
Computationally efficient—runs in under 3 minutes on 50K evaluations, making it practical for real deployment compared to infeasible brute-force search
Comprehensive empirical analysis across multiple platforms (Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench), evaluation types (human vs. LLM-as-judge), and top-k values

Detailed investigation beyond aggregate results: identifies specific influential evaluations, inspects dropped content (Table 2), analyzes model involvement patterns (Appendix B), and shows correlation between score proximity and robustness
Clear presentation with well-structured notation, helpful visualizations (especially Fig. 6), and reproducible research with public code release
Striking empirical finding that 0.02% of data can flip top ranking demonstrates the severity of the fragility in crowdsourced evaluation systems
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily an application of existing AMIP methodology to BT models; Proposition 3.1 is straightforward, and the core insight (reducing to pairwise robustness) lacks substantial technical depth
Gap between theory and practice: analysis uses tie-free BT models while Chatbot Arena actually implements weighted BT models that handle ties, potentially affecting conclusions

Approximation quality not thoroughly validated—no empirical comparison of AMIP predictions vs. actual ranking changes, no controlled experiments demonstrating when/why the influence function approximation fails

Shallow causal analysis—documents sensitivity but provides limited insight into whether close rankings reflect inherent difficulty in distinguishing model quality or specific data collection practices

Limited proposed solutions—suggests directions (confidence ratings, expert evaluation) but provides no empirical validation, cost-benefit analysis, or concrete implementation guidance for improvements
Narrow empirical scope: only two platforms, MT-Bench is small (3,355 evaluations), historical Chatbot Arena snapshot, unclear generalizability to other ranking systems (Elo-based, weighted schemes)

Methodological gaps: greedy algorithm is heuristic and could miss non-robust pairs; no systematic ablation studies; no statistical testing or confidence intervals; limited sensitivity analysis across different α values

Causal interpretation concerns—the dramatic framing (handful of preferences) emphasizes worst-case adversarial scenarios that differ substantially from realistic data corruption, which should be clarified
Presentation issues: Figure 1 has overlapping labels; Figure 3 category descriptions could be clearer; missing systematic analysis of how evaluation density and temporal variation affect robustness

strengths: Addresses timely and practically important problem of LLM leaderboard reliability with direct relevance to practitioners
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple platforms, domains (Chatbot Arena, MT-Bench, Vision/Search/Webdev Arenas), and evaluation types (human and LLM-as-judge)
Technically sound methodology that extends AMIP to Bradley-Terry models through principled logistic regression formulation
Practical tool with exact verification—uses AMIP for candidate identification but performs exact BT refitting to verify all reported non-robustness findings (no false positives)
Efficient implementation (<3 minutes on 50k evaluations) with actionable output identifying specific prompts/responses responsible for ranking flips
Clear presentation with honest discussion of limitations; Appendix thoroughly documents methodology
Insightful analysis connecting narrow BT score margins to fragility (Figure 18), suggesting data quality issues rather than fundamental flaws
Contrast between uniform and worst-case data dropping (Table 3) provides valuable perspective on robustness properties
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily adapts existing AMIP method (Broderick et al. 2020) to BT models through straightforward logistic regression; Theorem B.1 is simple observation without deep theoretical insight

Possibility of false negatives due to masking effects where multiple data points jointly influence outcomes; greedy pairwise approach may miss non-robustness instances, making negative robustness claims inconclusive

Incomplete understanding of root causes—while paper identifies narrow score margins as explanatory factor, doesn't establish whether this reflects fundamental limitations, data quality issues, or statistical noise
Qualitative analysis of dropped preferences uses only 2 examples with GPT-5.1 judgment; lacks systematic human evaluation of whether dropped preferences are genuinely atypical

No validated solutions provided—Section 6 suggests improvements (expert annotators, curated prompts, richer feedback) but provides no empirical validation; MT-Bench robustness attribution is correlational
AMIP approximation quality not fully characterized—while exact refitting provides verification, paper doesn't quantify how close AMIP predictions are to true optima or provide error bounds
Limited scope of generalization—all systems tested use Bradley-Terry models; unclear how findings extend to alternative ranking methods (Elo, Glicko) or multi-way comparisons

Incomplete practical guidance for practitioners—paper doesn't explain how users should interpret or act on fragility of closely-ranked models; implications for leaderboard design and interpretation underexplored
Statistical significance not fully addressed—doesn't compare fragility to expected noise levels or explore whether better statistical modeling could naturally accommodate this variability
No code availability mentioned; reproducibility could be enhanced with clearer documentation of hyperparameters and AMIP approximation settings
